For EACH of the following areas you must discuss at least three specific named mechanisms in real depth: (1) SSA construction, (2) alias analysis, (3) register allocation, (4) inlining, (5) escape analysis, (6) loop vectorization, (7) instruction scheduling, (8) loop optimizations . Use precise standard terminology for every mechanism you name. Be exhaustive: a shallow mention of an area does not count as covering it.

response.content:
This is a self-contained knowledge task. Delegating to child agents would not reduce effort or risk, so I will write the brief directly.

# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al.'s dominance-frontier algorithm** is the canonical construction. It proceeds in two phases. First, φ-function placement: for each variable v, φ-functions are inserted at the iterated dominance frontier DF⁺(Defs(v)), the least fixed point of the dominance frontier operator applied to v's definition sites. The dominance frontier of a block X is the set of blocks Y such that X dominates a predecessor of Y but does not strictly dominate Y itself. Second, renaming: a preorder walk of the dominator tree maintains a stack of reaching definitions per variable, rewriting uses to the top-of-stack name, pushing at each definition, and popping on exit from the block. Dominators themselves are typically computed with the Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm using semidominators, or in practice with the Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy iterative dataflow formulation, which is simpler and often faster on real control-flow graphs despite worse asymptotic bounds.

**Pruned and semi-pruned SSA** refine placement. Minimal SSA as produced by Cytron's algorithm inserts φ-functions even for variables dead at the join point. Pruned SSA runs liveness analysis first and only places a φ for v at block B if v is live-in at B. Semi-pruned SSA (Briggs et al.) is the engineering compromise: it computes the set of "non-local" names, variables live across any basic block boundary, via a cheap single pass, and skips φ-insertion entirely for block-local temporaries. This captures most of the pruning benefit without a full liveness computation, which matters because the vast majority of temporaries in compiler-generated IR are block-local.

**Braun et al.'s on-the-fly construction** (the algorithm used by Cranelift and several JITs) builds SSA directly during AST-to-IR translation without computing dominance frontiers at all. Each block tracks local variable writes. A use is resolved by `readVariable`: if the block has a local definition, use it; otherwise recurse into predecessors. Blocks are "sealed" once all predecessors are known. Reads in unsealed blocks create operandless φ-functions that are completed at sealing time. The algorithm removes trivial φ-functions (those whose operands are all the same value or the φ itself) recursively, yielding minimal SSA on reducible CFGs, and the trivial-φ removal doubles as on-the-fly copy propagation.

**Sreedhar–Gao DJ-graph placement** computes φ-placement in linear time per variable using the DJ-graph, the dominator tree augmented with "join" edges (CFG edges not in the tree). Rather than precomputing full dominance frontiers, which can be quadratic in size, it answers iterated-dominance-frontier queries on demand by a bottom-up walk over dominator-tree levels using a piggybank data structure. This is the basis of LLVM's `IDFCalculator`, used both in initial construction via `mem2reg` promotion of allocas and in passes like `SSAUpdater`-style repair.

Worth noting on the exit path: **SSA destruction** is nontrivial because naive copy insertion for φ-operands breaks in the presence of critical edges and the "lost copy" and "swap" problems. Sreedhar's Method III and Boissinot et al.'s revisited out-of-SSA translation handle φ-congruence classes and parallel-copy sequentialization correctly.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis** models each pointer assignment as a subset constraint: `p = &x` yields x ∈ pts(p), `p = q` yields pts(q) ⊆ pts(p), and loads/stores yield constraints conditioned on current points-to sets (complex constraints). Solving is a dynamic transitive closure over the constraint graph, cubic in the worst case. Practical implementations depend on cycle elimination, since constraint cycles imply points-to-set equality: Hardekopf–Lin's Lazy Cycle Detection and Hybrid Cycle Detection, plus offline variable substitution to merge pointer-equivalent variables before solving, make million-line programs tractable. Points-to sets are stored as sparse bitmaps or BDDs. Andersen's is flow-insensitive and (usually) context-insensitive but is the precision baseline for whole-program analysis; GCC's IPA points-to and field-sensitive intra-TU analysis follow this design.

**Steensgaard's unification-based analysis** trades precision for near-linear time. Assignments unify equivalence classes with union-find rather than generating subset constraints: `p = q` merges the pointed-to classes of p and q. The result is almost-linear, O(n·α(n)), making it viable as an always-on analysis, but unification is bidirectional, so a single assignment can conflate unrelated objects program-wide. Hybrids exist: Das's one-level flow keeps directionality at the top level of the points-to hierarchy and unifies below it, recovering much of Andersen's precision at near-Steensgaard cost.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA)** derives disjointness from the source language's typing rules instead of from value flow. Under C/C++ strict aliasing (C11 6.5p7), an lvalue of type T may not access an object of unrelated effective type, so accesses through `int*` and `float*` cannot alias. LLVM encodes this as TBAA metadata: a tree (or DAG, for struct-path TBAA) of type descriptors where two accesses may alias only if one's type descriptor is an ancestor of the other's, with struct-path TBAA additionally tracking field offsets within aggregates. TBAA is unsound for programs that violate the type rules, which is why `-fno-strict-aliasing` exists, and it is deliberately conservative around `char*` and unions.

**LLVM's BasicAA** is a stateless, intraprocedural, rule-based analyzer that resolves most queries in practice. It decomposes GEP (getelementptr) chains into base-plus-scaled-index-plus-constant-offset form and proves non-aliasing of accesses off the same base from offset/size arithmetic. It applies decidability facts: distinct `alloca`s and globals never alias; a `noalias` argument (the LLVM semantics backing C `restrict`) doesn't alias other memory not derived from it; pointers from `noalias` return functions (e.g., `malloc`) are distinct from pre-existing pointers. It also exploits escape information: a non-escaping alloca cannot alias memory accessed through an unrelated pointer. BasicAA sits in a chain with TBAA, scoped-noalias metadata, and SCEV-based AA (which disambiguates loop-indexed accesses via recurrence analysis), with `AAQueryInfo` aggregating the meet of all responses: NoAlias, MayAlias, PartialAlias, MustAlias, plus mod/ref information for calls.

Two dimensions cut across all of these: **flow sensitivity** (respecting statement order, usually recovered cheaply by running a flow-insensitive analysis over SSA, since SSA gives flow sensitivity for top-level pointers for free) and **context sensitivity** (k-CFA call-strings, object sensitivity for OO languages, or CFL-reachability formulations à la Sridharan–Bodík that compute demand-driven, context-sensitive answers for individual queries).

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin–Briggs graph coloring** reduces allocation to K-coloring of the interference graph, where nodes are live ranges and edges connect simultaneously-live ranges. The phases: Build (construct interference from liveness), Simplify (repeatedly remove nodes of degree < K onto a stack, since they're trivially colorable), Spill decision, and Select (pop and assign colors). Chaitin spilled pessimistically whenever simplification blocked. Briggs's key fix is **optimistic coloring**: push high-degree nodes anyway and only spill if no color is actually available at Select time, which helps because a node's neighbors often share colors. Spill choice uses a cost/degree heuristic (estimated spill cost, weighted by loop depth, divided by degree); spilling inserts loads/stores, and the whole allocator iterates until it colors. **Coalescing** removes copies by merging nodes: Briggs's conservative coalescing merges a,b only if the merged node has fewer than K neighbors of significant degree; George's iterated coalescing interleaves coalescing with simplification using a complementary test (every neighbor of a either interferes with b or has insignificant degree), and both guarantee coalescing never turns a colorable graph uncolorable.

**Linear scan** (Poletto–Sarkar) abandons the interference graph for speed: sort live intervals by start point, sweep once, maintain an active set, and when registers run out, spill the interval with the furthest endpoint. Original linear scan over-approximates lifetimes as single intervals. **Second-chance binpacking** (Traub et al.) and the Wimmer–Franz formulation used in HotSpot's C1 and early LLVM add lifetime holes, interval splitting at arbitrary points, and use-position-driven spill decisions, allowing a value to live in different locations over its lifetime. Linear scan is the standard choice for JIT baseline/mid-tier compilers because it is O(n log n) and single-pass.

**LLVM's greedy allocator** (`RAGreedy`) is a priority-based global allocator over SSA-derived live intervals. Live ranges are dequeued by a priority (size, spill weight, locality) and assigned; on conflict, a range may **evict** a lower-weight range, triggering its reallocation. The distinctive machinery is **live-range splitting** driven by a Hopfield-network-style region-split cost model over the edge-bundle graph: a global range is split into per-region ranges so that spill code lands on cold edges rather than inside hot loops. It also performs **rematerialization**, recomputing cheap values (constants, address computations) at use sites instead of reloading from a spill slot, and last-chance splitting before resorting to a true spill.

**SSA-based register allocation** (Hack et al.) exploits the theorem that interference graphs of programs in SSA form are chordal, and chordal graphs are colorable in polynomial time by a perfect elimination order, which a dominator-tree walk provides. Consequence: spilling can be decided *before* coloring (lower MaxLive to K, then coloring is guaranteed to succeed), fully decoupling the spill/color/coalesce subproblems that Chaitin-style allocators entangle. The cost moves into SSA destruction, where φ-related parallel copies must be sequentialized and coalesced. **PBQP** (partitioned Boolean quadratic programming) allocation deserves mention as the third family: it encodes register constraints, including irregular architectures with register pairs and aliasing register files, as cost matrices and solves with reduction rules plus heuristics; it ships in LLVM as an alternative allocator.

## 4. Inlining

**Bottom-up, cost-model-driven inlining** is the production baseline (LLVM's inliner). The pass walks the call graph in strongly-connected-component postorder, so callees are fully simplified before their callers consider them, making size estimates honest. Each call site gets a `InlineCost` computed by symbolically simulating the callee with the actual arguments bound: constant arguments trigger constant folding, branch elimination, and dead-block elision inside the simulation, so the estimated size is the *post-specialization* size, not the static size. The cost is compared against a threshold adjusted by bonuses and penalties: hint bonuses (`inline` keyword, hot callsites), the vector/last-call bonuses, penalties for setjmp, indirect branches, and a large static size cap. SCC-local iteration lets inlining expose further inlining. The dual knob, callee-size threshold versus caller-growth budget, controls the code-size/locality trade-off; unbounded inlining degrades instruction-cache behavior, which is why `-Os` lowers thresholds.

**Profile-guided and priority-based inlining** replaces static heuristics with measured hotness. With PGO (instrumentation or sample-based, e.g., AutoFDO/SamplePGO), hot call sites get raised thresholds and cold sites get aggressively lowered ones, and context-sensitive sample profiles (CSSPGO) attribute samples to inlined instances so second-build decisions match first-build inlining. MLGO-style learned policies and the ModuleInliner's priority-queue ordering (process hottest sites globally first, rather than SCC-locally) belong to this family. In JITs the analogue is tiered compilation: HotSpot inlines based on invocation counters and per-call-site receiver profiles collected by the interpreter and C1.

**Speculative inlining with devirtualization** handles indirect and virtual calls. Class hierarchy analysis (CHA) proves a virtual call monomorphic when only one implementor is loaded; when CHA is inconclusive, the compiler uses receiver-type profiles to perform **guarded inlining**: emit a type check (or method-address check) that falls through to the inlined body on the expected receiver and to the virtual dispatch, or in HotSpot an **uncommon trap** that deoptimizes back to the interpreter, on the slow path. Deoptimization makes the speculation free of a residual slow path in the compiled code and is invalidated if class loading breaks the CHA assumption. The AOT analogue is LLVM/GCC indirect-call promotion (ICP) from value profiles, and whole-program devirtualization (WPD) under LTO using vtable type metadata.

**Partial inlining and outlining** target functions dominated by an early-exit fast path: the compiler splits the callee, inlines only the hot prefix (e.g., the "already initialized, return" check), and leaves the cold remainder as an outlined call. GCC's `fnsplit` and LLVM's PartialInliner implement this; the related CodeExtractor-based cold-region outlining (and machine outlining for size) is the inverse transformation. This recovers most of the branch-elimination benefit of inlining a large function at a fraction of the growth.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph escape analysis** (Choi et al., the JVM-lineage formulation) builds, per method, a graph of object nodes, reference variables, and field edges, and classifies each allocation as GlobalEscape (reachable from a static field or another thread), ArgEscape (reachable from arguments/return, escapes the method but not the thread), or NoEscape. The analysis is interprocedural via method summaries: a callee's connection graph is specialized at each call site by mapping phantom argument nodes to actual argument subgraphs. HotSpot C2's escape analysis is in this family. The classification feeds three distinct optimizations: stack or scalar allocation for NoEscape objects, **lock elision** (synchronization on a non-thread-escaping object is removed, since no other thread can contend), and elimination of GC write barriers or allocation-site merging.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SRA/SROA)** is the payoff transformation: a NoEscape, non-aliased object whose fields are statically resolvable is exploded into one SSA value per field, eliminating the allocation entirely, not merely moving it to the stack. Fields then participate in constant propagation, register allocation, and dead-code elimination like any scalar. LLVM's SROA pass does the same for `alloca`s (after inlining has made the "object" local), using the fact that a non-escaping alloca with only direct loads/stores can be promoted via mem2reg; escape here is defined by address-taken-ness surviving into calls or stores of the pointer itself.

**Partial escape analysis** (Stadler/Kotzmann–Mössenböck lineage; implemented in GraalVM) is flow-sensitive virtualization: instead of a whole-method escape verdict, the compiler tracks each allocation's state along each path and keeps the object **virtual** (a bag of field values in SSA registers) until the precise program point where it escapes, if ever. On the escaping path only, it **materializes** the object, allocating and storing the current field values; deoptimization points get the virtual state recorded in frame metadata so the interpreter can rematerialize the object on deopt. This wins on the common pattern where an object escapes only on a cold exception path: the hot path pays no allocation at all. It composes with lock elision (locks on virtual objects are deferred and applied only on materialization).

**Region-based and lifetime inference analyses** form the third strand in AOT settings: Go's escape analysis is a whole-package, flow-insensitive but field-sensitive analysis over an abstract assignment graph with "escape heights," deciding stack versus heap per allocation site (observable via `-gcflags=-m`), with outlives relationships driven by loop depth and address flow into sinks (returns, globals, closures, channel sends). Tolman/Ruf-style thread-escape analyses and ML-family region inference (Tofte–Talpin) are the academic ancestors; the common structure is a reachability problem over a points-to abstraction specialized to the question "does lifetime exceed frame/thread?"

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**Classic loop (superword-wide) vectorization with dependence analysis** transforms a scalar loop into one processing VF lanes per iteration, legal only if no lexically-backward loop-carried dependence has distance < VF. Dependence testing works on affine subscripts: the **GCD test** (a dependence requires the GCD of coefficients to divide the constant term), **Banerjee inequalities** (bounding the dependence equation over the iteration space), and exact tests like the **Omega test** (integer programming) classify pairs with direction vectors (<, =, >) per loop level. Reductions (sum, min/max) are vectorized by recognizing the recurrence and generating a horizontal reduction in the epilogue; first-order recurrences and induction variables get dedicated widening rules. LLVM's LoopVectorize additionally uses **SCEV** (scalar evolution) to prove subscripts affine and compute trip counts, and a cost model comparing scalar versus vector cost per VF, including choosing an interleave factor (unroll-and-jam of the vector body) to hide latency.

**Runtime guards: alias checks and versioning.** When static dependence analysis fails (e.g., possibly-overlapping pointer arguments), the vectorizer emits **loop versioning**: a runtime overlap check comparing `base+trip*stride` ranges of each may-aliasing pointer pair, branching to the vector loop if disjoint and the scalar loop otherwise. The same mechanism covers stride==1 checks for symbolic strides and wrap-around (overflow) checks SCEV couldn't discharge. Quadratic growth in the number of check pairs is the practical limiter, hence memory-check thresholds. Tail handling is the sibling problem: a scalar epilogue for trip%VF remainder iterations, or **tail folding by masking**, where the main loop is predicated and processes the remainder under a mask, which is the default on scalable-vector targets (SVE, RVV) using active-lane predicates and `vsetvl`-style length control.

**If-conversion and masked/predicated vectorization.** Control flow inside the loop body is converted to data flow: branches become masks (compare results), stores become masked stores or select-then-store, and loads on conditional paths become masked loads, legal only if speculation is safe or the target has faulting-suppressed masked loads (AVX-512, SVE first-faulting). Divergent constructs that can't be if-converted (early exits with side effects) block vectorization; recent work handles some early-exit loops via first-faulting loads. **VPlan**, LLVM's vectorizer infrastructure, makes all of this explicit: candidate vectorization strategies are built as VPlan recipes (widen, replicate, predicate, interleave-group) and costed against each other before any IR is touched, replacing the legacy one-shot legality+cost structure.

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization** (Larsen–Amarasinghe) vectorizes straight-line code rather than loops: it finds isomorphic independent scalar instruction trees, seeded from adjacent memory accesses or reduction chains, and rolls them into vector instructions, inserting gather/insertelement glue where operands don't pack cleanly. The cost model charges for shuffles and extracts, and the bottom-up tree-building with a lookahead for operand reordering (commutative operand swapping to maximize isomorphism) determines profitability. SLP catches manually unrolled loops, structure-of-arrays arithmetic, and complex-number kernels that loop vectorization misses, and the two passes are complementary in LLVM's pipeline. Interleaved access vectorization, handling AoS patterns via `vldN/vstN` or shuffle networks for stride-2/3/4 groups, rounds out the memory-layout toolkit.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling** is the workhorse for basic-block (and region) scheduling. Build the data dependence DAG over instructions with edges weighted by latency (true, anti, and output dependences; memory edges inserted conservatively where alias analysis can't disambiguate), then greedily emit from a ready list each cycle, choosing by a priority function, classically the **critical path height** (maximum latency-weighted path to a DAG sink), with tie-breakers for register pressure, successor count, and resource usage. A machine model (per-opcode latency and functional-unit reservation tables, or itineraries) gates issue; hazard recognizers model structural hazards. Modern backends schedule bidirectionally (LLVM's MachineScheduler walks top-down and bottom-up, picking the better candidate) and treat **register-pressure reduction** as a co-equal objective with latency, tracking pressure sets against register-file limits because a "faster" schedule that forces spills loses, which is why pre-RA and post-RA scheduling are separate passes with different priorities.

**Modulo scheduling (software pipelining)** overlaps loop iterations to sustain throughput on statically scheduled or wide-issue machines. Compute the minimum **initiation interval**: II = max(ResMII, RecMII), the resource bound (uses of the most-contended functional unit divided by its count) and the recurrence bound (for each dependence cycle, ⌈latency/distance⌉). **Iterative modulo scheduling** (Rau) then tries to place each operation in a modulo reservation table of II slots, backtracking by ejecting conflicting operations, incrementing II on failure. **Swing modulo scheduling** (Llosa et al., implemented in LLVM's MachinePipeliner) orders nodes to minimize register lifetimes by scheduling along recurrences alternately early and late. The transformed loop needs a prologue and epilogue to fill/drain the pipeline, and **modulo variable expansion** or rotating register files (Itanium) to resolve the overlapping lifetimes of the same variable from different in-flight iterations.

**Trace and superblock scheduling** extend scheduling scope across branches for ILP machines. **Trace scheduling** (Fisher) picks the likeliest acyclic path through the CFG using profile data, schedules it as one long block, and inserts **compensation code** in off-trace blocks to repair moves of instructions above splits or below joins. **Superblock scheduling** (Hwu et al., IMPACT) simplifies this by tail duplication: a superblock has one entry and multiple exits, so no join-point bookkeeping is needed; speculation above branches remains, requiring either safe speculation (no faulting), poison/sentinel schemes, or hardware support. Hyperblocks add if-conversion with predication to subsume unbiased branches entirely. These techniques are also where **global code motion** meets scheduling: Click's GCM formulation schedules from a sea-of-nodes IR by choosing each node's block between its earliest (dominator of inputs) and latest (LCA of uses) legal placement, preferring low loop depth.

## 8. Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)** hoists computations whose operands are invariant across iterations into the preheader, and sinks stores that are only needed after the loop. Legality for loads requires that the location is invariant (no aliasing store in the loop, per AA/MemorySSA) and that hoisting doesn't introduce a fault on a zero-trip path, handled by proving the load dereferenceable, by guaranteed-execution analysis (the instruction dominates all exits), or by loop guards/rotation ensuring the body executes. **Store promotion** is the aggressive form: a memory location loaded and stored every iteration is promoted to a register for the loop's duration with a single preheader load and exit store, requiring must-alias and thread-safety reasoning (no data-race introduction, hence `MustExecute` and alignment/atomicity checks). LICM composes with **loop rotation** (transforming while-loops into do-while guarded form), which creates the preheader-dominates-body structure most loop passes assume.

**Induction variable optimizations and strength reduction.** IV analysis identifies basic IVs (i = i + c recurrences) and derived IVs (affine functions of basic IVs), canonically via SCEV's add-recurrence chains {start,+,step}. **Strength reduction** replaces multiplications by the loop index in addressing (a[i] → pointer increment) with additions; **linear function test replacement** rewrites the exit comparison in terms of the reduced IV so the original can die; IV widening eliminates sign-extensions by proving no-overflow (nsw/nuw flags, trip-count bounds); and loop-strength-reduction proper (LLVM's LSR) solves a global formula-selection problem choosing IV representations that minimize register pressure and match target addressing modes. Operator strength reduction on SSA (Cooper–Simpson–Vick OSR) is the clean SSA-graph formulation of the classic Allen–Cocke–Kennedy technique.

**Restructuring transformations: unrolling, interchange, fusion/distribution, tiling, unswitching.** **Unrolling** replicates the body by factor U, reducing branch overhead and exposing ILP/scheduling freedom, in runtime-trip-count form with an epilogue or prologue remainder, and in full form when trip counts are small constants; unroll-and-jam unrolls an outer loop and fuses the resulting inner-loop copies, key for register tiling. **Loop interchange** swaps nest levels to make the innermost stride unit (column-major vs row-major traffic) or to move a parallelizable/vectorizable loop innermost; legality requires the permuted direction-vector matrix to remain lexicographically non-negative. **Fusion** merges conforming adjacent loops to improve temporal locality and reduce overhead (legal absent fusion-preventing dependences); **distribution (fission)** does the reverse, splitting a loop so that the vectorizable statements separate from a recurrence, and is how LLVM's LoopDistribute enables partial vectorization. **Tiling/blocking** strip-mines and interchanges to create cache-sized working sets for loop nests like matmul, with tile-size selection driven by cache capacity/associativity models. **Loop unswitching** hoists a loop-invariant conditional out of the loop by cloning the loop per branch arm (trivial unswitching for guaranteed-taken cases, full unswitching with cost caps for code growth). The unifying generalization is the **polyhedral model** (Polly, GCC Graphite, Pluto scheduling): iteration domains as Z-polyhedra, transformations as affine schedules found by ILP to optimize locality and parallelism simultaneously, with exact dependence analysis via parametric integer programming, at the cost of applying only to static control parts (SCoPs).

---

**Cross-cutting note.** These areas are coupled in pipeline order: SSA quality determines what alias and escape analysis can see; alias precision gates LICM, vectorization legality, and scheduler memory edges; inlining is the enabler that turns interprocedural facts into intraprocedural ones for escape analysis and SROA; and register allocation sits in tension with scheduling and unrolling, which both raise register pressure. Production compilers resolve the phase-ordering problem empirically, with pass managers interleaving simplification (InstCombine, GVN) between the passes above.

Answer: The brief above covers all eight requested areas, each with three or more named mechanisms treated in depth: SSA construction (Cytron dominance-frontier construction, pruned/semi-pruned variants, Braun on-the-fly construction, Sreedhar–Gao DJ-graphs, SSA destruction), alias analysis (Andersen, Steensgaard, TBAA, LLVM BasicAA, flow/context sensitivity), register allocation (Chaitin–Briggs coloring with Briggs/George coalescing, linear scan and second-chance binpacking, LLVM greedy with eviction/splitting, SSA-chordal and PBQP allocation), inlining (bottom-up cost-model inlining, profile-guided/priority inlining, speculative guarded inlining with devirtualization and deoptimization, partial inlining), escape analysis (connection graphs, SROA/scalar replacement, partial escape analysis with materialization, Go-style lifetime inference, lock elision), loop vectorization (dependence-test-based loop vectorization, runtime alias checks and versioning with tail folding, if-conversion/masked predication under VPlan, SLP), instruction scheduling (list scheduling, iterative/swing modulo scheduling, trace/superblock scheduling and global code motion), and loop optimizations (LICM with store promotion, IV strength reduction/LSR, unrolling, interchange, fusion/distribution, tiling, unswitching, and the polyhedral model).
